title: I used AI tools to help ship my first game after 30 years of wanting to make one - here’s what I used and how I disclosed it
author: PhilosophyNumerous45
selftext:
Long time lurker, first time poster. I've   
wanted to make a game since I was a kid   
playing DOS platformers in the early 90s.   
This year I finally did it.

Arcane Dash is a retro pixel platformer   
inspired by Commander Keen, Jazz Jackrabbit   
and Hocus Pocus. I'm a solo developer and   
used AI assistance for some assets.

Here's exactly what I used AI for:

\*\*AI assisted:\*\*  
\- Music and soundtrack (generative AI)  
\- Cutscene artwork  
\- Game logo  
\- Translations (11 languages, machine   
  translation reviewed by me)

\*\*Human made:\*\*  
\- All 36 levels (hand designed by me)  
\- Programming (Java)  
\- Character and enemy sprites (these were done by a contractor artist)  
\- Sound effects  
\- Level editor (built from scratch)  
\- All marketing materials

I disclosed everything on the Steam store   
page as Valve requires. Honestly I was   
nervous about the reaction but most people   
have been supportive or indifferent.

The game is in Steam Next Fest from   
October 19th and Episode 1 is completely   
free if you want to try it:

https://store.steampowered.com/app/5173190/Arcane\_Dash\_\_A\_Pixel\_Adventure/

Happy to answer questions about the AI   
tools I used or the disclosure process! Thanks for reading 😊

comments.author: No_Experience_3443
comments.body:
I have to say it's probably the most detailed description of ai use within a steam page. Usually people stay very vague to make it look like it's not 90% of the art that's ai generated

Tho i'm starting to wonder what place these games will have. Indie development was already hell because the market is oversaturated and people have less money than before for games.

But now everyone makes quick prototype that they call game and try to sell them after 1 week to 3 months of development thanks to ai trying to make a quick buck.

I don't know how long it took to make your game but soon everyone will probably assume that games made with heavy ai for any art ( music included ) are just rushed prototypes, that is if they even find your game

replies.author: PhilosophyNumerous45
replies.body:
Really fair points and I appreciate the   
honest feedback. To answer your question, this took about a year of evenings and weekends to build. 36 hand designed levels, custom level editor, custom pixel font, all programming from scratch in Java.

The AI assisted with music and some artwork   
which I couldn't afford to commission   
properly as a solo dev with no budget.   
I take your point about market perception   
though, it's a legitimate concern for   
the industry.

replies.author: ForgotTheSnare
replies.body:
I love the fact you felt the enjoyment of taking an idea to completion after years of frustration. I certainly know the feeling! I have been a frustrated wannabe indie game dev all my life. If your main goal is to satisfy that frustration and you used AI to get there then I don’t think there is anything wrong with it.

However if it is to make some money out of it, the story is different imo.

The point you are responding to is valid. I think there is a market for slop and quickly rushed ideas. But likely outside of Steam as a platform. I think the slop fits more the Lord Farsquaad TikTok generation.

But on Steam, you’re going to struggle. I looked at the video clip and the jumps don’t feel right, but I haven’t played so I don’t know. I like the nostalgia behind it, but to make something new and old at the same time is one hell of a problem to solve.

Not to mention your game will compete with tons of other platformers and it’s oversaturated. People’s money is going to go to games like Well Dweller.

That said I wish you good luck. And whatever happens you would have learned things that you can take to your next project!

replies.author: PhilosophyNumerous45
replies.body: Appreciate the honest take. The jump physics were something I've iterated on a lot. Tight and snappy was a deliberate choice over floaty, there is a movement smoothing option in the options menu in the full game to make things more floaty. Episode 1 is free so anyone can judge for themselves. 🙂

replies.author: Professional_Ask3718
replies.body:
On the market for slop concept, I recently whipped up a 3 prompt game that i consider complete garbage, noone will ever see it but its quickly become my kids favorite game. It taught me one lesson: Slop built specifically for one person can be pretty effective, but its still not good for a bigger audience.


I too am working on a game ive wanted to make since I was a kid, and yes some ideas will fall flat, but i think this kind of fresh creativity is exactly what the games industry needs right now. It was becoming stagnant and only focusing on sequals as the risk of new ideas resulting in a flop would cost many people their jobs

replies.author: PhilosophyNumerous45
replies.body: That's a really lovely way to put it. Good luck with your game! The fact you've wanted to make it since you were a kid means it'll have something real in it. 🙂 AI is just another tool at the end of the day, it’s a means to an end.

comments.author: trai1er_dude
comments.body:
You've just wasted a lot of time and a $100 steam fee plus whatever other expenses you had. Aside from that I don't believe that all the programming is human made if you're using AI to that extent in other areas, that's fine but you should either not admit any AI use or be completely honest about it. 

The problem is that your achievement is massively diminished by the fact you used AI, a great analogy i heard was it's like saying you did a marathon but you drove in a car. Literally anybody can create a game like yours nowadays just by typing a load of prompts and it completely undermines the achievement and makes it basically worthless.

replies.author: PhilosophyNumerous45
replies.body:
The programming, all 36 levels, the level   
editor and the pixel font are entirely   
human made and transparently documented on the Steam page. I work with code every day in my job so the code is very much mine.

AI assisted with music and some artwork, tools I used as a solo dev with no budget.

Also worth noting — you're on r/aigamedev 😄

The game exists. People are playing it.   
That's not wasted time in my book. 🧙

replies.author: Square_Reason_6490
replies.body: He’s a hater so whatever. Good job and great way to share what was ai and what’s not, good luck on the sales and I don’t think you wasted 100$ if you gaining that much experience

replies.author: PhilosophyNumerous45
replies.body:
Thank you! Really appreciate the support 🧙

The experience alone has been worth every   
penny - shipping something you've dreamed   
about for 30 years is hard to put a price on.

And honestly the learning curve outside   
the code has been just as valuable, I’ve learned so much about the non game dev related stuff like marketing, social media, Steam, press   
outreach. Things nobody tells you about   
when you decide to make a game! 😄

replies.author: trai1er_dude
replies.body:
meh i'm sorry i don't believe you, i also work every day with code in my job and i'm forced to use AI which i don't mind. If you're doing any coding professionally now, very very few people are doing it without the assistance of AI as from a business perspective it's much more efficient/productive to use it. I'm not saying AI wrote all your code but i would bet it assisted you, at the bare minimum you're using AI solutions when you get stuck, now nobody uses stackoverflow anymore, AI responses (even if it's just the AI google response) are much more precise and bespoke to your specific problem. Again i said you should just lie completely or be completely honest about it. I've got no issue with AI use and admittedly you're not forced to disclose AI coding on steam. 

The problem lies when the product is very basic, the use of AI diminishes that product further to the extent that almost nobody will buy it and is therefore essentially a waste of time. Admittedly you've undoubtedly learned some things but anybody can literally create a basic 2d platformer nowadays with literally a few prompts.

comments.author: Puchufu
comments.body: Looks very cool. I'm also in the midst of making my own game and struggle with whether to just make it for my friends to enjoy or market it. It's a passion project for sure and have had an amazing time seeing it come to life. I've tried getting friends to help with artwork and music, but interest has always fizzled so I'm looking toward giving it a shot with AI tooling for those areas. What worked best for you? And what kind of sub levels did you need for best results and ROI for the time spent?

replies.author: PhilosophyNumerous45
replies.body:
Firstly, thanks for the comment! 

**For music:** I used Claude web to generate MIDI files, then manually edited and refined them in Rosegarden. (Free MIDI software) It gave me a starting point I could actually shape into something that fit each level's feel, way faster than composing from scratch, but still required real hands-on work to get right.

**For cutscene artwork:** ChatGPT (free tier) for the illustrated cutscene art. Lots of iteration to nail the style, but doable on zero budget.

**For in-game sprites (player, bosses):** Contractor artist from Fiverr - AI wasn't precise enough for the pixel work.

**ROI:** The biggest win as a solo dev is just *having* music and art at all. Time cost is real (lots of back-and-forth), but money cost was near zero. Wouldn't have shipped without these tools. Free tiers got me surprisingly far, ChatGPT free for the cutscene art, and Claude's free tier for the MIDI work. The main cost was time, not money.

The part AI couldn't replace: all 36 levels built and designed manually by me (this was the most time consuming process), and 10 years of Java experience to actually read, understand, and validate the code, even where Claude Code helped with sections, you still need to know what you're looking at or it falls apart fast.

Hope this breakdown helps!
